title: Why Do We Put Up Christmas Trees? The Real Story
hook: For a few hundred years, the Christmas tree was mostly a German-speaking habit, and much of Britain and America barely knew it.
thumbnail_picture: Big close-up on the right of a huge glowing candlelit fir tree hung with red apples and gilded nuts in a Victorian parlor, a wide-eyed Victorian girl in a long dress gasping with delight beside it, deep dark warm shadows filling the empty left third.
description:
Why do we put up Christmas trees? Follow the real story of the Christmas tree from ancient evergreen boughs to Riga, Strasbourg, Queen Victoria and a famous 1848 engraving.
Christmas tree history explained: how one evergreen branch crossed Europe and America through royal marriages, migration and a newspaper picture.

Sources and further reading:
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Christmas tree"
- Penne Restad, Christmas in America: A History (Oxford University Press, 1995)
- Royal Collection Trust, material on Queen Victoria and Prince Albert's Christmas trees
- Illustrated London News, December 1848, engraving of the royal family at Windsor

real story of the christmas tree
why do we have christmas trees

scenes.narration: For a few hundred years, this glowing tree was a German-speaking habit. Britain and America barely knew it existed.
scenes.caption: A GERMAN HABIT
scenes.picture: A small candlelit fir tree on a wooden table in a cozy German parlor, a family of four gazing at it, frosty window behind them, warm golden glow, 1600s clothes.

scenes.narration: So what if it had stayed that way? What if one picture, printed one December, had never existed?
scenes.caption: WHAT IF?
scenes.picture: An empty corner of a plain Victorian living room, a lone armchair beside a frosty window, nothing decorated, a puzzled grey cat staring at the bare corner.

scenes.narration: No tree in the corner. No lights, no presents piled underneath. Just holly on the mantel and a cold house.
scenes.delivery: quiet, bleak, then a beat of wonder
scenes.caption: NO TREE
scenes.picture: A dim Victorian parlor, holly sprigs on a stone mantel above a small coal fire, a child in a long white nightgown standing and looking at the empty bare corner.

scenes.narration: But here's the strange part. Why would anyone drag a whole tree into the house in the dead of winter?
scenes.caption: WHY INDOORS?
scenes.picture: A bundled man in a brown wool coat hauling a tall fir tree through a narrow cottage doorway while his wife in a shawl watches, snow falling.

scenes.narration: The answer starts with one evergreen branch, and the long road it traveled to reach your living room.
scenes.caption: ONE BRANCH
scenes.picture: Close-up of a single dark green fir branch heavy with fresh snow, soft blue winter light, a blurred snowy forest in the background.

scenes.narration: Start in a forest in midwinter, where many trees have dropped their leaves and turned gray.
scenes.caption: MIDWINTER
scenes.picture: A wide snowy forest at dusk full of bare gray oaks and birches, a few dark green fir trees standing among them, pale winter sky.

scenes.narration: But not the fir. It stays green through the snow, through the dark, through everything.
scenes.caption: STILL GREEN
scenes.picture: One lone green fir tree glowing against deep snow while the bare black trees around it stand leafless, cold blue twilight, no people.

scenes.narration: To people living by firelight, that was likely a sign of life in the dead of winter. Something out there refused to die.
scenes.caption: LIFE IN WINTER
scenes.picture: Three villagers in furs and rough wool crouched around a campfire at night, one holding up a green fir branch, faces lit orange and amazed.

scenes.narration: So green boughs mattered. Romans decorated their homes with them around Saturnalia, their wild party, and the New Year Kalends.
scenes.caption: SATURNALIA
scenes.picture: A Roman atrium with green garlands wrapped around the columns, oil lamps glowing, two people in tunics laughing and passing bronze wine cups.

scenes.narration: Many northern Europeans seem to have brought evergreens indoors in winter too, though the evidence is thin.
scenes.caption: GREEN INDOORS
scenes.picture: Inside a smoky timber longhouse, fir branches tied to the rafters, villagers in wool tunics feasting at a long table with bread and bowls, firelight.

scenes.narration: But nobody wrote down exactly why. So be careful with tidy stories about druids and sacred trees. Mostly, that's guesswork.
scenes.caption: MOSTLY GUESSWORK
scenes.picture: A woman in a plain wool cloak tying green fir sprigs above a wooden door in a snowy village, breath steaming in the cold, thatched roofs behind.

scenes.narration: Then the branch hit trouble. Around the year 200, the Christian writer Tertullian scolded believers for hanging laurel and lamps on their doors during pagan festivals.
scenes.caption: TROUBLE
scenes.picture: A stern man in a plain Roman tunic pointing angrily at a doorway hung with laurel garlands and oil lamps, a worried neighbor beside him, North Africa, 200 AD.

scenes.narration: Anything that smelled pagan was in danger. So the evergreen did what survivors do. It changed its meaning.
scenes.caption: A NEW MEANING
scenes.picture: Two villagers in medieval cloaks carefully setting a green fir branch beside the stone altar inside a small candlelit church, quiet and reverent.

scenes.narration: Then came the apples. In late-medieval Germany, plays about Adam and Eve were staged on December twenty-fourth.
scenes.caption: EDEN PLAYS
scenes.picture: Medieval townspeople in hooded cloaks watching two actors in simple costumes on a wooden stage in a snowy German town square, torches burning.

scenes.narration: And Eden needed a tree. It's often said the Eden tree was an evergreen hung with apples, since in winter a fir was the only green one around.
scenes.caption: THE PARADISE TREE
scenes.picture: A green fir tree hung with shiny red apples standing alone on a wooden medieval stage, torches burning beside it, snow on the ground.

scenes.narration: Historians think this Paradise tree fed into the Christmas tree. For the first time, the evergreen had a story the church could live with.
scenes.caption: PARADISE TREE
scenes.picture: Townspeople with awed faces gathered around a fir tree hung with red apples, glowing torchlight, night, medieval German square.

scenes.narration: So families copied the play at home: a fir in the parlor, red apples, and thin white wafers.
scenes.caption: HOME COPIES
scenes.picture: A mother in a long wool dress and two children hanging red apples and round white wafers on a small fir tree in a timber-framed German cottage room.

scenes.narration: Early ornaments were apples, wafers, nuts, paper roses. Glass baubles, which appeared in the 1800s, are often said to imitate those apples.
scenes.caption: FIRST ORNAMENTS
scenes.picture: Close-up of a hand hanging a shiny red apple on a green fir branch, soft candlelight, a snow-dusted window blurred behind.

scenes.narration: By the early 1500s the branch had grown into a whole tree, and it was walking into city squares.
scenes.caption: INTO THE CITY
scenes.picture: A snowy market square in a German town with half-timbered houses, two workers in wool coats carrying a tall fir across the cobblestones.

scenes.narration: Riga tradition says that in 1510, young unmarried merchants of the Brotherhood of Blackheads, in today's Latvia, raised a tree.
scenes.caption: RIGA CLAIMS 1510
scenes.picture: Young merchants in dark caps and tunics raising a tall decorated fir in a snowy square of Riga ringed by tall gabled houses, 1510.

scenes.narration: The story goes that they danced around it, and then set the whole thing on fire.
scenes.caption: THEN THEY BURNED IT
scenes.picture: Young merchants in dark caps and tunics dancing in a circle around a blazing fir tree at night in a snowy Riga square, sparks rising.

scenes.narration: Riga proudly claims the first one. Tallinn, up the coast, says it had one in 1441. Nobody can prove either.
scenes.caption: WHO WAS FIRST?
scenes.picture: Two old merchants in fur hats arguing and pointing in opposite directions across a snowy Baltic harbor square, gabled houses and ships behind.

scenes.narration: But the clearest early snapshot comes from Strasbourg, in the year 1605, and it sounds very familiar.
scenes.caption: STRASBOURG, 1605
scenes.picture: A snowy street of half-timbered houses in Strasbourg, 1605, with the tall red sandstone cathedral spire rising behind, a few people in warm cloaks.

scenes.narration: There, an unnamed writer recorded that people set up fir trees in their parlors, hung with paper roses, apples, wafers and sweets.
scenes.caption: ROSES AND APPLES
scenes.picture: A timber-framed parlor with a fir tree decorated with red paper roses, apples and sweets, a family in 1600s clothes admiring it, warm light.

scenes.narration: Look a little further back. Alsace towns such as Sélestat, in 1521, and later Strasbourg, wrote down rules protecting young firs around Christmas.
scenes.caption: TOO MANY TREES
scenes.picture: A forester in a 1500s wool coat frowning at a row of freshly sawn fir stumps in a snowy Alsace forest, axe on his shoulder.

scenes.narration: Which hints the habit was catching on. Every December, more families seem to have wanted a tree of their own.
scenes.caption: CATCHING ON
scenes.picture: A line of horse carts stacked with fir trees rolling through a stone city gate in falling snow, drivers bundled in cloaks, Strasbourg, 1600s.

scenes.narration: Next came light. By the late 1600s and early 1700s, Germans were clipping candles to their trees.
scenes.caption: CANDLES
scenes.picture: Close-up of white wax candles burning on dark green fir branches, golden glow filling a dark room, tiny flames reflecting on needles.

scenes.narration: Legend says Martin Luther started it, after walking home under glittering stars. It's a lovely story with no proof.
scenes.caption: A LOVELY LEGEND
scenes.picture: A scholar in a dark cap and cloak, Martin Luther in the 1520s, walking a snowy forest path under a sky full of bright stars, looking up in wonder.

scenes.narration: But real candles on dry pine needles? Terrible idea. Fires were common.
scenes.caption: FIRE RISK
scenes.picture: A parlor where a fir tree has caught fire from its candles, flames climbing the branches, a shocked family in 1700s clothes stepping back.

scenes.narration: So many families kept water nearby, and the tradition survived anyway.
scenes.caption: WATER READY
scenes.picture: A wooden bucket of water beside a lit candle tree, a small girl in a 1700s dress watching the flames, her face glowing, calm room.

scenes.narration: But until the late 1700s, the tree stayed mostly in German-speaking lands. Outside them, it looked strange.
scenes.caption: STUCK IN GERMANY
scenes.picture: A German village at dusk with glowing windows in every house, beyond it a dark empty road winding across snowy hills, nobody in sight.

scenes.narration: In Puritan Massachusetts, you could be fined for celebrating Christmas at all. A tree would have been a scandal.
scenes.caption: PURITAN RULES
scenes.picture: A stern Puritan magistrate in a black hat and white collar wagging his finger at a nervous farmer outside a plain wooden meeting house, 1659.

scenes.narration: In England, Christmas meant holly, ivy and mistletoe. A whole fir tree in the house? Very foreign.
scenes.caption: HOLLY ONLY
scenes.picture: An English cottage interior with holly and ivy draped on the oak beams and a bunch of mistletoe above the door, hearth fire crackling.

scenes.narration: So the branch found a back door: marriage. In 1761, a German princess named Charlotte married King George the Third.
scenes.caption: A ROYAL WEDDING
scenes.picture: A young German princess, Charlotte, in a pale silk gown, stepping off a ship onto an English harbor quay in 1761, curious and nervous.

scenes.narration: Around Christmas 1800, Queen Charlotte had a small lit yew tree set up for a children's party at her Windsor home.
scenes.caption: QUEEN CHARLOTTE
scenes.picture: A Georgian drawing room where children in silk clothes gather around a small candlelit yew tree on a table, a smiling queen in a powdered wig watching.

scenes.narration: But it didn't spread. The branch needed a famous face to carry it out.
scenes.caption: NOT YET
scenes.picture: A snowy Georgian country house at night, one tall window glowing warm gold, dark yew trees and dark grounds all around, no people.

scenes.narration: Enter a girl named Victoria. Around 1832, she wrote in her journal about trees hung with lights and sweets.
scenes.caption: YOUNG VICTORIA
scenes.picture: A thirteen-year-old girl with light brown hair in a simple white dress, Princess Victoria, writing in a journal at a small desk, a glowing lit tree behind her, joyful.

scenes.narration: She became queen. In 1840, she married her German cousin, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg.
scenes.caption: QUEEN AND ALBERT
scenes.picture: Queen Victoria, a short young woman with brown hair parted in the middle, in a white wedding gown, and Prince Albert, a young man with brown hair and short sideburns in a dark frock coat, side by side in a grand chapel, 1840.

scenes.narration: Albert grew up with candlelit trees every winter. He made them a family fixture.
scenes.caption: ALBERT'S TREE
scenes.picture: Prince Albert, a young man with brown hair and short sideburns in a dark frock coat, carrying a fir tree through a stone castle corridor, grinning, snow on his shoulders.

scenes.narration: So every Christmas, the royal family dressed trees in candles, sweets, little toys and gilded nuts.
scenes.caption: ROYAL TREES
scenes.picture: Close-up of a table-top fir tree covered in candles, sweets, tiny toys and gilded nuts, glittering golden light in a castle room.

scenes.narration: Then, in December 1848, one picture changed everything.
scenes.caption: DECEMBER 1848
scenes.picture: A busy Victorian print workshop where an engraver bends over a small wooden block with fine tools, lamp light, ink-stained hands.

scenes.narration: A newspaper, the Illustrated London News, printed an engraving of the royal family gathered around their tree.
scenes.caption: THE ENGRAVING
scenes.picture: Queen Victoria, a short young woman with brown hair parted in the middle, in a dark silk dress, and Prince Albert, with brown hair and short sideburns in a dark frock coat, smiling beside three young children around a glowing table-top Christmas tree.

scenes.narration: The queen was the biggest celebrity of her age. If she had a tree, a tree was fashionable.
scenes.caption: THE ORIGINAL INFLUENCER
scenes.picture: A cheering Victorian crowd in bonnets and top hats on a London street, waving at an open royal carriage carrying a young queen in a dark silk dress.

scenes.narration: Trees were already catching on among the fashionable. After the print, every family with a little money wanted to look like that picture.
scenes.caption: EVERYONE WANTS ONE
scenes.picture: A father in a top hat and long coat carrying a small fir home through a foggy London street while two excited children in wool coats run beside him.

scenes.narration: Shops began selling ornaments, and trees arrived by the cartload. By the 1860s they were common in many middle-class British homes.
scenes.caption: A NEW HABIT
scenes.picture: A Victorian market stall stacked with small fir trees and shiny glass ornaments, shoppers in coats and bonnets browsing, snow falling.

scenes.narration: Across the ocean, the branch had been quietly living in German immigrant homes, mostly unnoticed.
scenes.caption: ACROSS THE OCEAN
scenes.picture: A German immigrant family in a log farmhouse hanging apples and cookies on a small fir tree, deep snow outside the window, Pennsylvania, 1830s.

scenes.narration: Then in 1850, an American magazine, Godey's Lady's Book, reprinted the royal picture.
scenes.caption: AMERICA, 1850
scenes.picture: Several American women in 1850s hoop dresses gathered in a parlor, admiring a small decorated Christmas tree with delighted faces.

scenes.narration: But the editors quietly removed the queen's tiara, so the family looked like any American household.
scenes.caption: THE TIARA VANISHES
scenes.picture: Close-up of an engraver's hands carving a tiny detail into a small wooden printing block with a fine steel tool, workshop lamp glowing.

scenes.narration: A royal custom had become an ordinary family one, and over the next few decades it caught on across America.
scenes.caption: ORDINARY FAMILIES
scenes.picture: A big American family in a farmhouse parlor gathered around a fir tree with homemade ornaments, children holding wooden toys, 1860s.

scenes.narration: In 1882, an associate of Thomas Edison, Edward Johnson, strung electric bulbs on a tree in New York.
scenes.caption: NEW YORK, 1882
scenes.picture: A fir tree in a New York brownstone window glowing with small red, white and blue electric bulbs, passersby gaping on a snowy street, 1882.

scenes.narration: Over the next few decades, electric lights made trees safer, and big community trees began to appear in town squares.
scenes.caption: TREES GO PUBLIC
scenes.picture: A very tall fir tree covered in electric lights in the middle of a snowy town square, children and parents in 1910s coats gazing up at it.

scenes.narration: So let's go back to that empty corner. Without the engraving, would Britain ever have got the tree? Probably, eventually.
scenes.caption: BACK TO THE CORNER
scenes.picture: A bare Victorian parlor corner with an armchair and holly on the mantel, a girl in a long dress peering at the empty space beside the chair.

scenes.narration: But it would've been slower, patchier, and maybe never the one thing nearly everyone does.
scenes.caption: SLOWER, PATCHIER
scenes.picture: A long snowy Victorian street at dusk, nearly every window dark, only one window glowing warm with the light of a Christmas tree.

scenes.narration: Traditions don't spread because they're ancient. They spread because someone everyone admires is seen doing them.
scenes.caption: WHY IT SPREAD
scenes.picture: Victorian shoppers in coats and bonnets pressed against a shop window, staring at a lit Christmas tree inside, wonder on their faces, snowy London.

scenes.narration: Look at what's in your corner: a Roman green bough, a medieval Eden prop, a royal wedding, a newspaper picture.
scenes.caption: IT'S ALL IN THERE
scenes.picture: A cozy modern living room with a decorated fir tree, red round ornaments and warm string lights, a couch and a sleepy dog on the rug.

scenes.narration: A German custom that crossed borders in trunks, in royal weddings, and in one famous engraving.
scenes.caption: CROSSING BORDERS
scenes.picture: A family of immigrants in 1850s clothes on the deck of a steamship holding bundled belongings and one small potted fir sapling, gray sea behind.

scenes.narration: And that evergreen branch? It's still doing the job it did in those frozen forests.
scenes.caption: THE BRANCH
scenes.picture: A lone snow-covered fir tree in a moonlit forest clearing, still deep green against white snow, stars above, no people.

scenes.narration: Reminding us, in the darkest week of the year, that something is still green.
scenes.caption: STILL GREEN
scenes.picture: Close-up of a child's hands hanging a small red ornament on a green tree branch in a warm room, golden light.

scenes.narration: That's why there's a tree in your living room in December. One branch refused to die, and a lot of people carried it.
scenes.caption: THE REAL STORY
scenes.picture: A snowy cottage at night in a forest clearing, one window glowing gold with the light of a decorated tree inside, quiet and peaceful.

narrator: Curious, thoughtful explainer, brisk, playful wonder, rising energy on the big what-if.

short.title: Why We Really Put Up Christmas Trees
short.description:
Why do we put a fir tree in our homes every December? It started with one London newspaper picture in 1848.
The surprising story of how a German habit became a worldwide tradition. Sources: Illustrated London News (1848); Godey's Lady's Book (1850); Bernd Brunner, Inventing the Christmas Tree.

scenes.narration: Christmas trees went worldwide largely thanks to one London newspaper picture from 1848.
scenes.caption: LONDON, 1848
scenes.picture: Queen Victoria, young woman with a dark hair bun and a small crown, in a blue silk gown, beside Prince Albert, tall young man with short brown hair and side whiskers in a dark coat, smiling at a small candlelit fir tree on a table with three children, warm Windsor Castle room, tall frame.

scenes.narration: For centuries before, the Christmas tree was just a German habit.
scenes.caption: A GERMAN HABIT
scenes.picture: A small fir tree on a wooden table, decorated with red apples and tiny lit candles, large and central, in a cozy timber-framed German room with a snowy window behind, a blurred family of four watching in the background, 1500s.

scenes.narration: In England, Christmas meant holly, so a tree indoors looked foreign.
scenes.caption: HOLLY ONLY
scenes.picture: A puzzled English man in a brown wool coat standing in a cottage doorway, staring at a big green fir tree, while green holly and ivy hang from dark oak beams behind him, glowing hearth fire, 1700s England.

scenes.narration: In 1840, England's Queen Victoria married her German cousin, Prince Albert, who loved candlelit trees.
scenes.caption: QUEEN AND ALBERT
scenes.picture: Queen Victoria, young woman with a dark hair bun, in a white wedding gown with an orange blossom wreath, and Prince Albert, tall young man with short brown hair and side whiskers in a dark formal coat, standing side by side smiling inside a grand stone chapel, 1840.

scenes.narration: So the royal family put up a tree every Christmas.
scenes.caption: ROYAL TREES
scenes.picture: Prince Albert, tall young man with short brown hair and side whiskers in a dark coat, grinning as he carries a green fir tree on his shoulder through a long stone castle corridor, snow on his shoulders, torch light, 1840s Windsor Castle.

scenes.narration: In 1848, the Illustrated London News printed a picture of their family around the tree.
scenes.caption: THE ENGRAVING
scenes.picture: An ink-stained Victorian engraver with rolled-up shirt sleeves and a leather apron, bending over a wooden printing block with a fine carving tool, lamp light glowing on his focused face, crowded London print workshop, 1848.

scenes.narration: Victoria was the biggest celebrity of her day, so everyone wanted her tree.
scenes.caption: THE INFLUENCER
scenes.picture: A delighted Victorian woman in a bonnet and long gray dress stopping on a foggy London street, holding up a folded newspaper, mouth open in a gasp, two blurred passers-by peeking over her shoulder, gas lamp, 1848.

scenes.narration: In 1850, an American magazine reprinted the picture.
scenes.caption: AMERICA, 1850
scenes.picture: Three American women in 1850s hoop dresses with ringlet hair, leaning close together over a page of a magazine in a Philadelphia parlor, delighted faces, a window with soft daylight, medium shot.

scenes.narration: But it removed the queen's tiara, so the family looked ordinary.
scenes.caption: TIARA VANISHES
scenes.picture: Close-up of an engraver's hands holding a fine steel tool, carving a tiny scratch on a small wooden printing block, brass lamp glowing beside it, wood shavings on the bench, 1850s Philadelphia workshop.

scenes.narration: So ordinary American families copied it too.
scenes.caption: EVERYONE COPIES
scenes.picture: A big American farm family in plain 1860s clothes, a father, mother and three children, laughing around a homemade fir tree with paper chains and popcorn strings, a child holding a wooden toy horse, farmhouse parlor.

scenes.narration: So that's why we have trees: an old German habit, spread around the world by one famous picture.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: A snowy log cottage at night in a dark pine forest clearing, one window glowing gold from a small decorated Christmas tree inside, smoke rising from the chimney, stars above, wide peaceful view, Germany.
